newsitem.title: USA: Motorola to cut jobs, capacity, posts weak results.
newsitem.headline: Motorola to cut jobs, capacity, posts weak results.

text.p: Motorola, Inc., posting poor third-quarter results, said late Monday it will reduce jobs and manufacturing capacity to cut costs as some of its businesses remain weak.

The telecommunications giant said its performance was hurt by a downturn in the semiconductor industry, competitive pressures, falling prices for its cellular phones, pagers and other products, and weaker sales on related items.

Profits fell by more than half to $206 million, or 34 cents a share, in the third quarter from $496 million, or 81 cents a share, in the year-ago period. Sales fell 5 percent to $6.5 billion from $6.9 billion.
Net margin on sales fell to 3.2 percent from 7.2 percent.

"Because of the continuing weakness in some of our businesses, primarily the Semiconductor Products Sector, the company is expanding cost-cutting actions already under way, including manufacturing and work force adjustments," said Christopher Galvin, president and chief operating officer.
"Specific actions are expected to be finalised during the fourth quarter and will have an adverse effect on fourth-quarter earnings.

Galvin attributed the decline in third-quarter earnings mainly to the recession in the semiconductor industry. The results seem worse because Motorola recorded a substantial net gain on the sale of certain assets in the 1995 third quarter, he said.
Motorola's Semiconductor Products Sector saw sales fall 19 percent to $1.8 billion in the third quarter. Orders slid 33 percent and operating profits plunged to break-even.
Orders were lower in all geographic regions from a year ago. Among major market segments, only automotive posted a gain in orders. Distributor orders were lower, it said.
All of the sector's technology groups experienced weaker orders. Orders for all product categories fell except sensor products, whose demand grew.
Motorola's General Systems Sector's sales fell 2 percent to $2.6 billion in the third quarter. Orders rose 13 percent and operating profits declined.
Cellular Subscriber Group orders grew while sales slid as the effect of higher unit shipments was offset by falling prices, Motorola said.
Cellular Infrastructure Group rose and orders increased significantly, due to strength in international markets.
Computer Group sales were lower but orders increased, it added. Motorola's stock rose $1 to $49.25 on the New York Stock Exchange.
